# Tevijja Sutta (DN 13 (PTS DN i 235))

**ID:** DN 13 (PTS DN i 235)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Tevijja Sutta
**PTS:** DN i 235
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0101m.mul12.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Challenging claims of authority rooted in the Vedas and mere report (*anussava*), the Buddha criticizes the ancient Vedic seers for claiming to know the way to a state and a deity they have never directly seen or experienced [Jayatilleke 1963; Ham 2016].

In place of Vedic ritual and reliance on traditional lore, the Buddha presents ethical discipline and the cultivation of the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) or immeasurables (*appamāṇa*)—radiating loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity in all directions—as the genuine way leading to rebirth in the realm of Brahmā [Ham 2016; Skorupski 1991; Martini 2011]. This meditative radiation is illustrated by the simile of a vigorous conch-shell blower whose sound effortlessly fills the four quarters [Martini 2011]. Uniquely among the first thirteen suttas of the *Dīghanikāya*, the sutta culminates in the *brahmavihāras* and rebirth in the Brahmā world without elaborating the higher ideal of arahantship [Kingsbury 2002; Norman 1983]. At the discourse's conclusion, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja declare themselves lay followers; the commentary (*Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, Sv 406) reads this episode as part of an unfolding sequence continued from the *Vāseṭṭha Sutta* (MN 98) and leading to their ordination in the *Aggañña Sutta* (DN 27) [Collins 1993].

A full parallel to the sutta exists in the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (DĀ 26). Modern computational analysis by DharmaNexus aligns segments of the text with Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (T 1) and *Madhyamāgama* (T 26) texts, as well as Sanskrit fragments from the *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Arthaviniścayasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, the sutta shares extensive formulaic material with the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta* (DN 9), *Subha Sutta* (MN 99), *Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta* (SN 42), and *Caṅkī Sutta* (MN 95) [DharmaNexus], including thirty-eight shared paragraphs drawn from the standard gradual training exposition established in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2) [Kingsbury 2002].
